topic: Balance training after 60: small habits that prevent falls

slides.headline: Balance is trainable at any age
slides.sub: Small daily habits that help you stay steady on your feet.

slides.title: Balance responds to practice
slides.body: Balance relies on your muscles, joints, eyes and inner ear working together. Like strength, it tends to improve when you challenge it regularly, and research suggests exercise can reduce falls in older adults.

slides.title: Habit 1: stand on one leg
slides.body: While the kettle boils, hold the bench and lift one foot. Aim for 10 to 30 seconds each side. As it gets easier, lighten your grip to fingertips, then let your hand hover.

slides.title: Habit 2: sit to stand, slowly
slides.body: Stand up from a chair without using your hands, then sit down slowly. Ten times, once or twice a day. Leg strength is a big part of catching yourself if you trip.

slides.title: Habit 3: make your home easier
slides.body: Good lighting on the way to the bathroom at night, no loose rugs, and a clear path down the hallway. Simple changes like these are easy to overlook.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See your GP or physio if you've had a fall, feel dizzy or unsteady when you stand up, notice new weakness in your legs, or find yourself avoiding walks because you're worried about falling.

caption:
Balance isn't something you simply lose with age. It's a skill, and it responds to practice.

Your muscles, joints, eyes and inner ear all work together to keep you steady. Research suggests regular exercise can reduce falls in older adults, and small daily habits add up: standing on one leg while the kettle boils, sit to stands, and clearing loose rugs at home.

If you've had a fall, feel dizzy when you stand, or are avoiding walks because you're worried about falling, have a chat with your GP or physio. If you have a chronic condition, ask your GP whether a chronic condition management plan suits you. It can give a Medicare rebate for up to 5 allied health visits a year, and there's usually a gap fee.
